implementation_notes: Modern C++ replaces both classic idioms with one construct: a function returning a reference to a function-local static, whose construction is deferred to the first call and, since C++11, guarded by the implementation so that it happens exactly once even from several threads (cppreference notes this guarantee and that it may be cheaper than the equivalent std::call_once). The nifty counter - aligned storage, placement new and a guard object per including translation unit - remains justified only for a header-defined global that must be usable before main or from other units' dynamic initializers (the std::cout case); C++17 inline variables usually replace even that. What neither form fixes is destruction: the static deinitialization order is still unspecified, so the accessor must not be used from another static object's destructor.
pitfalls: If the constructor throws, the guard is not flipped and the next call retries initialization; repeated failures can look like a loop and partially executed side effects can repeat.
Static deinitialization order is not fixed by this idiom: using the accessor during the destruction of another static object touches an object whose lifetime may already have ended.

The nifty counter depends on the counter and buffer being constant-initialized (zero) at load time and needs properly aligned storage plus placement new (std::aligned_storage itself is deprecated in C++23); prefer an inline variable or a constexpr-constructible object.

Function-local statics are initialized under a guard variable, so every call performs a load-and-branch even after initialization, and building with statics made non-thread-safe (or hand-rolling double-checked locking) reintroduces races.
A function-local static cannot be reset, which makes the accessor's state hard to isolate between tests.

variants.name: std::call_once with a never-destroyed heap object
variants.implementation_notes: Where the object must not be destroyed, or where its destructor would race with other statics' destructors, construct it once on the heap and never delete it: the C++ FAQ's pointer form leaks on purpose, which is harmless for memory the OS reclaims at exit but wrong if the destructor must flush or commit something. std::call_once also documents a useful difference from a function-local static: if the callable throws, the flag is not flipped, so a later call retries the initialization.
pitfalls: The destructor never runs, so any side effect it would have (flush, unregister, close) is silently skipped.
Prefer the function-local static unless 'never destroyed' is actually required; call_once adds an explicit flag and a pointer indirection for the same effect.

variants.name: Nifty (Schwarz) counter for header-defined globals
variants.idiom_name: per-translation-unit guard object + placement new into aligned storage
variants.implementation_notes: The classic pattern from More C++ Idioms: the header exposes the object as a reference into aligned storage and defines a static guard instance in every translation unit that includes it; the first guard's constructor placement-news the object and the last guard's destructor destroys it, so the object is alive from before the first possible use in any unit until after the last. Keep it for the case it was invented for - a header-defined global that other units' static initializers may use and that cannot become a C++17 inline variable - because it is the only form here that also bounds destruction to last use.
pitfalls: Getting the placement wrong (alignment, object lifetime rules) is undefined behaviour, and std::aligned_storage is deprecated in C++23.
The trick only works because nifty_counter is zero-initialized during load; if the guard needs dynamic initialization it is back inside the fiasco it was meant to fix.
